newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmakers bring home the bacon in pet projects.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmakers bring home the bacon in pet projects.

text.p: A Pentagon study of the Northern Lights, a study of brown tree snakes, and a mysterious foundation are among the billion dollars in special projects that lawmakers quietly voted to pay for this week.

Republican Sen. John McCain of Arizona, who combs each money bill for wasteful spending, chided fellow lawmakers Monday for trying to reap political gains in November by sending $2.4 billion in special projects to their states.
"It never ceases to amaze me how innovative and creative my colleagues can be in creating and earmarking funds for these pork-barrel projects," McCain said before the vote.

The projects were added to a huge 1997 spending bill approved Monday with almost no debate just hours before an Oct. 1 deadline. The money was essential to keep the government operating in the new 1997 fiscal year.

The private Citizens Against Government Waste said it identified many others in the 2,000-page bill including 20 National Forest Service construction projects, 20 forest service land purchases, numerous land exchanges that government agencies had not sought.

The Republican and Democratic leaders of the Pork Busters Coalition in the House were unable to scrutinize the bill before it cleared the House because copies were not made available, and no amendments were allowed, a House aide said.

In the first year of Republican congressional control, fiscal 1996 appropriations bills were trimmed nearly fat-free but the lure of coming elections was too tempting for elected officials to avoid sending money home. It was also a last chance. Next year President Clinton will be able to veto specific projects in spending bill thanks to new line-item veto powers.

"The (bill) is too sweet a target for people to resist. There has been a lessening of the zeal in this election year," McCain told Reuters. Next year he will send Clinton a list of suggested items to veto.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, R-Mississippi, admitted Congress added many items this year in fear they would not survive once Clinton has the line-item veto.
"A few items here and there managed to get in there -- on their merits," Lott said with a chuckle.

While one lawmaker's pork is another's worthy project, the usual definition is money thrust upon agencies by a small group of lawmakers for activities that have not been cleared by the administration or congressional committees.
Democrat Tom Daschle of South Dakota, Minority Leader of the Senate, said Thursday that the practice of offering money for specific projects was not necessarily wrong so long as they are scrutinized.
"We can't categorically condemn them all. But I do believe there ought to be greater scrutiny," he told reporters.
Among the items McCain identified as spending that should have been examined in brighter light were:
-- $10 million for Defense Department's electric vehicle research.
-- $1.9 million to supervise the Teamsters' election.
-- $8.5 million for an environmental institute at the University of New Hampshire, home state to Appropriations subcomittee chairman Judd Gregg, R-N.H.
-- $60 million fund to pay telecommunications companies for aiding in law enforcement.
-- $3 million for the unidentified WVATC Foundation's outreach program. "Nobody knows what it is," McCain said.

-- $1 million to continue research on eradication of brown tree snakes found in Southeast Asian countries in anticipation of the possible need to eradicate them as an invasive species in the United States.
-- $15 million for aurora borealis, or Northern Lights, research at the Pentagon.

Asked what he expected the Pentagon would gain from its $15 million of the Northern Lights, McCain replied: "I am sure many young officers on watch will want to know more about the aurora borealis rather than watch TV."
